cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does FTP data use?
cards.answer: TCP 20
cards.explanation: File Transfer Protocol data channel (active mode).
cards.example: An FTP client downloads a file; the server opens the data connection from port 20 in active mode.
cards.tip: FTP uses TWO ports: 21 = control (commands), 20 = data.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does FTP control use?
cards.answer: TCP 21
cards.explanation: FTP control connection for commands and authentication (username/password in clear text).
cards.example: ftp 192.0.2.10 connects to TCP 21 and logs in.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does SSH / SCP / SFTP use?
cards.answer: TCP 22
cards.explanation: Encrypted remote CLI access; SCP and SFTP also run over SSH.
cards.example: ssh -l admin 10.0.0.1 from a PC to a router configured with 'transport input ssh'.
cards.tip: SSH (22) replaced Telnet (23): secure comes first, one number lower.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does Telnet use?
cards.answer: TCP 23
cards.explanation: Unencrypted remote CLI access.
cards.example: Packet capture of a Telnet session shows the password in clear text.
cards.tip: Telnet = 23 = 'clear as day' — never use it on production networks.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does SMTP use?
cards.answer: TCP 25
cards.explanation: Sending/relaying email between mail servers.
cards.example: A mail server forwards a message to another domain's MX server on TCP 25.
cards.tip: SMTP Sends Mail To People — port 25.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does TACACS+ use?
cards.answer: TCP 49
cards.explanation: Device-administration AAA; encrypts the entire payload.
cards.example: Switches authenticate administrators against Cisco ISE using TACACS+.
cards.tip: TACACS+ is TCP (49) — both start with T.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does DNS use?
cards.answer: UDP/TCP 53
cards.explanation: Name resolution; UDP for normal queries, TCP for zone transfers and large responses.
cards.example: nslookup www.cisco.com sends a UDP 53 query to the configured resolver.
cards.tip: DNS 53 uses BOTH transports — a classic trick question.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does DHCP server use?
cards.answer: UDP 67
cards.explanation: DHCP server listens on UDP 67.
cards.example: A DHCP Discover is sent from 0.0.0.0:68 to 255.255.255.255:67.
cards.tip: Server 67 comes before client 68 — the server is 'first'.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does DHCP client use?
cards.answer: UDP 68
cards.explanation: DHCP client receives offers/acks on UDP 68.
cards.example: The client's lease negotiation uses source port 68.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does TFTP use?
cards.answer: UDP 69
cards.explanation: Trivial FTP: no authentication; used to copy IOS images and configs.
cards.example: copy running-config tftp: on a router.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does HTTP use?
cards.answer: TCP 80
cards.explanation: Unencrypted web traffic.
cards.example: Browsing http://192.168.1.1 to reach a device web GUI.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does POP3 use?
cards.answer: TCP 110
cards.explanation: Retrieving email from a server (downloads mail).
cards.example: A mail client downloads messages from a POP3 server.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does NTP use?
cards.answer: UDP 123
cards.explanation: Clock synchronization.
cards.example: ntp server 192.0.2.1 makes a router sync time over UDP 123.
cards.tip: NTP keeps time: 1-2-3, like counting seconds.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does IMAP use?
cards.answer: TCP 143
cards.explanation: Accessing email stored on a server (mail stays on server).
cards.example: A phone and laptop both see the same mailbox via IMAP.
cards.tip: IMAP 143 keeps mail on the server; POP3 110 downloads it.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does SNMP (agent) use?
cards.answer: UDP 161
cards.explanation: Manager polls agents with Get/Set requests.
cards.example: An NMS sends SNMP GetRequest to a switch on UDP 161.
cards.tip: 161 = polls, 162 = traps (the 'next' number goes to the manager).

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does SNMP trap/inform use?
cards.answer: UDP 162
cards.explanation: Agents send unsolicited Traps/Informs to the manager.
cards.example: A switch sends a linkDown trap to the NMS on UDP 162.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does BGP use?
cards.answer: TCP 179
cards.explanation: Border Gateway Protocol peering.
cards.example: Two ISPs establish an eBGP session over TCP 179.
cards.tip: BGP is the only common routing protocol that runs over TCP.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does LDAP use?
cards.answer: TCP/UDP 389
cards.explanation: Directory access (e.g., Active Directory lookups).
cards.example: ISE queries AD via LDAP for group membership.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does HTTPS use?
cards.answer: TCP 443
cards.explanation: HTTP over TLS (encrypted web, REST APIs).
cards.example: Catalyst Center's REST API is accessed via HTTPS 443.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does Syslog use?
cards.answer: UDP 514
cards.explanation: Sending log messages to a syslog server.
cards.example: logging host 192.0.2.50 sends messages over UDP 514.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does IKE (IPsec) use?
cards.answer: UDP 500
cards.explanation: Internet Key Exchange negotiates IPsec security associations.
cards.example: Two VPN gateways start IKE negotiation on UDP 500.
cards.tip: IKE 500; NAT-T moves IPsec to UDP 4500.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does IPsec NAT-T use?
cards.answer: UDP 4500
cards.explanation: Encapsulates IPsec ESP in UDP when NAT is present.
cards.example: A remote user behind a home router uses NAT-T on UDP 4500.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does RADIUS authentication use?
cards.answer: UDP 1812
cards.explanation: RADIUS authentication/authorization (legacy 1645).
cards.example: A WLC sends 802.1X credentials to ISE on UDP 1812.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does RADIUS accounting use?
cards.answer: UDP 1813
cards.explanation: RADIUS accounting (legacy 1646).
cards.example: ISE records session start/stop on UDP 1813.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does CAPWAP control use?
cards.answer: UDP 5246
cards.explanation: Lightweight AP to WLC control channel (DTLS-encrypted).
cards.example: An AP joins a WLC using CAPWAP control on UDP 5246.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does CAPWAP data use?
cards.answer: UDP 5247
cards.explanation: Lightweight AP to WLC client data tunnel.
cards.example: Client traffic in Local mode is tunneled to the WLC on UDP 5247.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does RDP use?
cards.answer: TCP 3389
cards.explanation: Remote Desktop Protocol to Windows hosts.
cards.example: An administrator RDPs to a jump server on TCP 3389.

cards.front: Which transport protocol and port number does NETCONF use?
cards.answer: TCP 830
cards.explanation: NETCONF over SSH for model-driven configuration.
cards.example: An automation script edits a router config via NETCONF on TCP 830.

cards.front: Port ranges: well-known, registered, and dynamic/ephemeral?
cards.answer: Well-known 0-1023 • Registered 1024-49151 • Dynamic/ephemeral 49152-65535
cards.explanation: Servers listen on well-known or registered ports; clients pick a temporary ephemeral source port for each connection.

cards.front: Name the four TCP/IP model layers and the OSI layers each covers.
cards.answer: Application (OSI 5-7) • Transport (4) • Internet (3) • Network Access/Link (1-2)
cards.explanation: The TCP/IP model is the practical internet stack; OSI is the 7-layer reference model.
cards.example: HTTP → Application; TCP → Transport; IP → Internet; Ethernet → Link.

cards.front: PDU names from Layer 4 down to Layer 1?
cards.answer: Segment → Packet → Frame → Bits
cards.explanation: Data is encapsulated with a header at each layer; Ethernet adds a trailer (FCS).
cards.example: A web request: data → TCP segment → IP packet → Ethernet frame → bits.
cards.tip: Some People Fear Birds: Segment, Packet, Frame, Bits.

cards.front: Which layer does each device primarily operate at: hub, switch, router?
cards.answer: Hub L1 • Switch L2 • Router L3
cards.explanation: Hubs repeat bits, switches forward frames by MAC, routers forward packets by IP. Multilayer switches also route (L3).
cards.example: A Layer 3 switch with SVIs routes between VLANs.
cards.tip: Hub repeats bits (L1), switch reads MACs in frames (L2), router reads IPs in packets (L3).

cards.front: Diagram: identify the layers in the encapsulation figure.
cards.answer: Data (L7) → TCP header (L4) → IP header (L3) → Ethernet header + FCS (L2) → bits (L1)
cards.explanation: Each header belongs to the layer that adds it. Only Layer 2 adds a trailer.
cards.example: Remove headers in reverse order at the receiver.
cards.tip: Headers stack outward: lower layers wrap higher layers.

cards.answer: Address Resolution Protocol

cards.answer: Neighbor Discovery Protocol

cards.example: NS/NA replace ARP request/reply.

cards.example: Hubs required CSMA/CD.

cards.tip: SVI up/up needs the VLAN plus an active port in it.

cards.answer: Dynamic Trunking Protocol
cards.explanation: Cisco protocol negotiating trunk status.
cards.example: dynamic auto + dynamic auto = access.

cards.answer: VLAN Trunking Protocol
cards.explanation: Cisco protocol that propagates VLAN definitions between switches.
cards.example: VTP modes: server, client, transparent (and off in v3).
cards.tip: Many networks use transparent mode to avoid accidental VLAN deletion.

cards.answer: Cisco Discovery Protocol
cards.explanation: Cisco Layer 2 neighbor discovery (60 s / 180 s holdtime).
cards.example: show cdp neighbors detail shows neighbor IPs.

cards.answer: Link Layer Discovery Protocol
cards.explanation: IEEE 802.1AB vendor-neutral discovery (30 s / 120 s).
cards.example: lldp run enables it globally.
cards.tip: Usually disabled by default on Cisco IOS.

cards.answer: Link Aggregation Control Protocol
cards.explanation: IEEE EtherChannel negotiation (active/passive).
cards.example: channel-group 1 mode active

cards.answer: Port Aggregation Protocol
cards.explanation: Cisco EtherChannel negotiation (desirable/auto).
cards.example: channel-group 1 mode desirable

cards.answer: Bridge Protocol Data Unit
cards.explanation: STP control message exchanged between switches.
cards.example: BPDU Guard err-disables a PortFast port that receives one.
cards.tip: Root bridge sends BPDUs every 2 s (hello).

cards.answer: Wireless LAN Controller
cards.explanation: Central controller for lightweight APs.
cards.example: Catalyst 9800 WLC manages APs via CAPWAP.
cards.tip: Split-MAC: real-time functions on AP, management on WLC.

cards.answer: Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points
cards.explanation: AP-to-WLC tunneling protocol.
cards.example: UDP 5246 control, 5247 data.

cards.answer: First Hop Redundancy Protocol
cards.explanation: Provides a redundant virtual default gateway (HSRP, VRRP, GLBP).
cards.example: Hosts use virtual IP 10.1.1.1 shared by two routers.

cards.answer: Hot Standby Router Protocol
cards.explanation: Cisco FHRP with active/standby routers.
cards.example: standby 1 ip 10.1.1.1
cards.tip: Default priority 100; no preempt by default.

cards.answer: Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol
cards.explanation: Standards-based FHRP with master/backup routers.
cards.example: Virtual MAC 0000.5E00.01xx.

cards.answer: Gateway Load Balancing Protocol
cards.explanation: Cisco FHRP that load-balances using multiple virtual MACs (AVG/AVF).
cards.example: AVG answers ARP with different AVF MACs.
cards.tip: G = Gateway load balancing = more than one forwarder.

cards.answer: Shortest Path First
cards.explanation: Dijkstra algorithm used by link-state protocols such as OSPF.
cards.example: Each router runs SPF on its LSDB.

cards.answer: Link-State Advertisement
cards.explanation: OSPF unit of topology information.
cards.example: Type 1 Router LSA, Type 2 Network LSA.

cards.answer: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
cards.explanation: Automatically assigns IP settings.
cards.example: DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Ack.

cards.answer: Network Address Translation
cards.explanation: Translates IP addresses (typically private to public).
cards.example: ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.10 203.0.113.10

cards.answer: Port Address Translation
cards.explanation: Many-to-one NAT using port numbers (NAT overload).
cards.example: ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/1 overload

cards.answer: Quality of Service
cards.explanation: Tools to prioritize and manage traffic during congestion.
cards.example: Voice in an LLQ priority queue.
cards.tip: QoS manages bandwidth; it doesn't add it.

cards.answer: Differentiated Services Code Point
cards.explanation: 6-bit Layer 3 QoS marking (0-63).
cards.example: Voice marked EF (46).

cards.answer: Class of Service
cards.explanation: 3-bit Layer 2 priority in the 802.1Q tag (PCP field).
cards.example: IP phones mark voice CoS 5.
cards.tip: CoS only exists on tagged frames.

cards.answer: Simple Network Management Protocol
cards.explanation: Monitoring/management using MIBs and OIDs.
cards.example: NMS polls UDP 161; traps to UDP 162.

cards.answer: Network Time Protocol
cards.explanation: Synchronizes clocks (UDP 123).
cards.example: ntp server 192.0.2.1
cards.tip: Lower stratum = closer to the reference clock.

cards.answer: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting
cards.explanation: Framework for controlling and auditing access.
cards.example: aaa new-model with TACACS+.
cards.tip: Who are you, what can you do, what did you do.

cards.answer: Access Control List
cards.explanation: Ordered permit/deny rules for filtering or identifying traffic.
cards.example: ip access-group WEB in

cards.answer: Dynamic ARP Inspection
cards.explanation: Validates ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding table.
cards.example: ip arp inspection vlan 10
cards.tip: DAI depends on DHCP snooping (or ARP ACLs).

cards.answer: Intrusion Prevention System
cards.explanation: Inline inspection that blocks malicious traffic.
cards.example: NGFW with IPS blocks an exploit attempt.

cards.answer: Multifactor Authentication
cards.explanation: Two or more factor types: know, have, are.
cards.example: Password + phone push notification.
cards.tip: Two passwords are still ONE factor.

cards.answer: Virtual Private Network
cards.explanation: Encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network.
cards.example: Site-to-site IPsec between branch and HQ.

cards.answer: Wi-Fi Protected Access
cards.explanation: Wi-Fi security family; WPA2 uses AES-CCMP, WPA3 uses SAE.
cards.example: WPA3-Personal replaces PSK with SAE.

cards.answer: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals
cards.explanation: WPA3-Personal key exchange resistant to offline dictionary attacks.
cards.example: Replaces the WPA2 PSK 4-way handshake weakness.

cards.answer: Software-Defined Networking
cards.explanation: Centralized control via a controller and APIs.
cards.example: Catalyst Center programs switches via southbound APIs.

cards.answer: Application Programming Interface
cards.explanation: Defined way for software to interact with other software.
cards.example: GET /dna/intent/api/v1/network-device
cards.tip: NBI to apps, SBI to devices.

cards.answer: Representational State Transfer
cards.explanation: Stateless API style over HTTP using verbs and URIs.
cards.example: POST creates, GET reads, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE deletes.
cards.tip: Stateless: every request carries its own auth/context.

cards.answer: JavaScript Object Notation
cards.explanation: Lightweight data format of objects {} and arrays [].
cards.example: {"hostname": "R1", "up": true}

cards.answer: YAML Ain't Markup Language
cards.explanation: Human-readable data format using indentation; used by Ansible playbooks.
cards.example: - name: Configure NTP

cards.answer: Virtual Extensible LAN
cards.explanation: Overlay encapsulation (MAC-in-UDP) used in SD-Access and data centers.
cards.example: SD-Access data plane uses VXLAN.

cards.answer: Locator/ID Separation Protocol
cards.explanation: SD-Access control plane mapping endpoints to locations.
cards.example: Fabric control-plane node runs LISP map server.
cards.tip: SD-Access: LISP control, VXLAN data, IS-IS underlay.

cards.answer: A set of devices that receive each other's Layer 2 broadcasts.
cards.explanation: Each VLAN is one broadcast domain; routers separate broadcast domains.
cards.example: Three VLANs on one switch = three broadcast domains.
cards.tip: Routers and VLANs break up broadcast domains; switches don't (within a VLAN).

cards.answer: A network segment where simultaneous transmissions can collide.
cards.explanation: Every switch port is its own collision domain; a hub is one shared collision domain.
cards.example: A 24-port switch has 24 collision domains.

cards.answer: The router IP a host uses to reach destinations outside its subnet.
cards.explanation: Must be in the same subnet as the host.
cards.example: Host 10.1.1.10/24 uses gateway 10.1.1.1.
cards.tip: Wrong gateway = local works, remote fails.

cards.answer: Latency is delay; jitter is the variation in delay.
cards.explanation: Voice tolerates ≤150 ms one-way delay and ≤30 ms jitter.
cards.example: Packets arriving 20, 80, 35 ms apart have high jitter.

cards.answer: One-to-one; one-to-all; one-to-group; one-to-nearest.
cards.explanation: IPv6 has no broadcast; anycast is a unicast address on multiple devices.
cards.example: FF02::1 (multicast to all nodes) replaces the IPv4 broadcast role.

cards.answer: Half duplex sends or receives at one time; full duplex does both simultaneously.
cards.explanation: Mismatch causes late collisions and CRC errors.
cards.example: Switch port full, PC half → slow, errors.
cards.tip: Match both ends or use auto on both.

cards.answer: Data center topology where every leaf connects to every spine.
cards.explanation: No leaf-to-leaf or spine-to-spine links; consistent hop count.
cards.example: Server → leaf → spine → leaf → server.

cards.answer: Access, distribution, core vs access + collapsed core.
cards.explanation: Collapsed core merges core and distribution for smaller campuses.
cards.example: A single building with two distribution/core switches.

cards.answer: A VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor; a container shares the host OS kernel.
cards.explanation: Containers are lighter and start faster.
cards.example: Docker container vs ESXi VM.

cards.answer: Virtual Routing and Forwarding: multiple isolated routing tables on one router.
cards.explanation: Allows overlapping IP space between customers.
cards.example: Customer A and B both use 10.0.0.0/24 on one PE router.
cards.tip: VRF = virtual router inside a router.

cards.answer: Power over Ethernet: switch (PSE) powers devices (PD) over the data cable.
cards.explanation: 802.3af 15.4 W, 802.3at 30 W, 802.3bt up to 60/90 W at the PSE.
cards.example: APs and IP phones powered by the access switch.

cards.answer: Weakness • potential danger • method that takes advantage of the weakness.
cards.explanation: Mitigation is the countermeasure that reduces risk.
cards.example: Unpatched IOS (vulnerability) + attacker (threat) + crafted packet (exploit).
cards.tip: V-T-E: the weakness, the danger, the weapon.

cards.answer: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, windowing, 20-byte header. UDP: connectionless, best effort, 8-byte header.
cards.explanation: TCP uses the 3-way handshake and acknowledgments; UDP has none.
cards.example: HTTPS uses TCP; voice (RTP) uses UDP.
cards.tip: TCP = Telephone call (setup first); UDP = postcard.

cards.answer: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK
cards.explanation: Establishes sequence numbers in both directions before data flows.
cards.example: Client SYN to 443, server SYN-ACK, client ACK.

cards.answer: Error reporting and diagnostics for IP (echo request/reply, unreachable, time exceeded).
cards.explanation: ping uses echo request/reply; traceroute relies on TTL time-exceeded messages.
cards.example: ping 8.8.8.8 → Echo Reply.
cards.tip: ICMP is Layer 3 helper; it has no ports.

cards.answer: Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge
cards.explanation: Discover and Request are broadcast by the client; relay converts them to unicast with ip helper-address.
cards.example: A PC boots and receives 10.1.10.50/24 from the server.
cards.tip: D-O-R-A like 'Dora the Explorer' exploring for an address.

cards.answer: Relays DHCP broadcasts as unicast to a DHCP server on another subnet.
cards.explanation: Configured on the interface facing the clients; sets giaddr so the server picks the right pool.
cards.example: interface g0/1 / ip helper-address 10.0.0.50
cards.tip: Helper goes where the HELP is needed: the client side.

cards.front: DNS record types A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, PTR?
cards.answer: A = IPv4 • AAAA = IPv6 • CNAME = alias • MX = mail server • PTR = reverse lookup
cards.explanation: PTR maps IP to name; others map names to data.
cards.example: www.example.com A 203.0.113.80.
cards.tip: AAAA = 4×A because IPv6 is 4× longer (128 vs 32 bits).

cards.answer: Distance from the reference clock; lower = more accurate.
cards.explanation: Stratum 0 = reference clock (GPS/atomic); stratum 1 server attaches to it.
cards.example: A router synced to a stratum 2 server becomes stratum 3.
cards.tip: Stratum is like floors from ground level.

cards.answer: Both are unsolicited agent → manager notifications; Inform is acknowledged, Trap is not.
cards.explanation: Informs are retransmitted if not acknowledged (SNMPv2c+).
cards.example: Link down event sent as Inform to the NMS.

cards.answer: %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC: description
cards.explanation: Severity number 0-7; e.g., %LINK-3-UPDOWN is severity 3 (Error).
cards.example: %OSPF-5-ADJCHG: Process 1, Nbr 2.2.2.2 ... FULL
cards.tip: The digit between dashes is the severity.

cards.answer: Policing drops/re-marks excess traffic; shaping buffers it (adds delay).
cards.explanation: Shaping is egress only; policing can be ingress or egress.
cards.example: ISP polices to 100 Mbps; customer shapes to 100 Mbps.
cards.tip: Police officers stop you; shapers make you wait.

cards.answer: 128 bits; 8 hextets of 4 hex digits separated by colons.
cards.explanation: Each hextet = 16 bits; each hex digit = 4 bits.

cards.answer: 1) Remove leading zeros in each hextet. 2) Replace ONE run of consecutive all-zero hextets with ::.
cards.explanation: Using :: twice is invalid because the length becomes ambiguous.
Remove leading zeros; the longest zero run (three hextets) becomes ::.
cards.example: A0 keeps its trailing 0 — only leading zeros go.
cards.tip: Pick the longest zero run for ::.

cards.answer: 2000::/3 (addresses beginning 2 or 3)
cards.explanation: Publicly routable; typically /48 site, /64 per subnet.
cards.example: 2001:DB8::/32 is reserved for documentation.

cards.answer: FC00::/7 (FD00::/8 in practice)
cards.explanation: Private-like; not routed on the internet.
Auto-created on every IPv6 interface; used for NDP and as routing next hops; never routed.
cards.example: FE80::1 on R1 Gi0/0
cards.tip: Every IPv6 interface has an FE80 address — it never leaves the link.

cards.answer: FF00::/8 • FF02::1 all nodes • FF02::2 all routers • FF02::5 OSPFv3 routers • FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx solicited-node
cards.explanation: IPv6 uses multicast instead of broadcast.
cards.example: Router Advertisements go to FF02::1.

cards.answer: 0250:56FF:FEAB:CDEF
cards.explanation: Split MAC, insert FFFE, flip the 7th bit of the first byte (00 → 02).

cards.answer: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration: host builds its address from the RA prefix + its own interface ID.
cards.explanation: Requires a router sending RAs ('ipv6 unicast-routing'). DNS info may come from RA (RDNSS) or stateless DHCPv6.
cards.example: ipv6 address autoconfig on a router interface.
cards.tip: Stateless = no server tracks the address.

cards.answer: 'ipv6 enable' creates only a link-local address; 'ipv6 address' assigns a global/ULA (and link-local automatically).
cards.explanation: Routing protocols can use link-local next hops.
cards.example: ipv6 address 2001:DB8:1::1/64

cards.answer: RS 133, RA 134, NS 135, NA 136, Redirect 137
cards.explanation: NS/NA replace ARP; RS/RA discover routers and prefixes.
cards.example: Host sends RS to FF02::2; router replies RA.
cards.tip: Router S/A before Neighbor S/A: 133-136 in order.

cards.answer: Normal 1-1005 (1002-1005 reserved) • Extended 1006-4094 • 0 and 4095 reserved
cards.explanation: VLAN ID is 12 bits (4096 values).
cards.example: vlan 2000 is an extended-range VLAN.

cards.answer: Default VLAN = VLAN 1 (all ports, undeletable). Native VLAN = untagged VLAN on an 802.1Q trunk (default 1).
cards.explanation: Best practice: change native VLAN to an unused VLAN on both ends.
cards.example: switchport trunk native vlan 99

cards.answer: 4 bytes: TPID 0x8100 (16 bits), PCP (3), DEI (1), VLAN ID (12)
cards.explanation: Inserted between source MAC and EtherType.
cards.example: Tagged frame max size 1522 bytes.

cards.answer: trunk + trunk/desirable/auto • desirable + desirable/auto. NOT auto + auto.
cards.explanation: Auto waits; desirable actively asks.
cards.example: Two new switches default dynamic auto → access link.

cards.front: Command to add VLAN 40 to a trunk's allowed list
cards.answer: switchport trunk allowed vlan add 40
cards.explanation: Without 'add' the list is replaced.
cards.example: Forgetting 'add' drops all other VLANs.

cards.front: Why doesn't 'show vlan brief' list trunk ports?
cards.answer: It lists access ports per VLAN; trunk VLANs appear in 'show interfaces trunk'.
cards.explanation: Use show interfaces trunk for allowed/active/forwarding VLANs.
cards.example: Gi0/1 trunk missing from show vlan brief.

cards.answer: encapsulation dot1Q <vlan-id> on each subinterface
cards.explanation: Subinterfaces Gi0/0.10, .20 each get an IP in their VLAN's subnet.
cards.example: interface g0/0.20 / encapsulation dot1Q 20 / ip address 10.20.0.1 255.255.255.0
cards.tip: Subinterface number need not match, but VLAN ID must.

cards.answer: Phone tags voice traffic with the voice VLAN (802.1Q); PC traffic behind it stays untagged in the access VLAN.
cards.explanation: Learned by the phone via CDP/LLDP.
cards.example: switchport access vlan 10 / switchport voice vlan 20
cards.tip: One port, two VLANs: data untagged, voice tagged.

cards.answer: LACP: active+active, active+passive. PAgP: desirable+desirable, desirable+auto. Static: on+on.
cards.explanation: passive+passive and auto+auto fail; on never mixes with negotiation.
cards.example: channel-group 1 mode active on both switches.
cards.tip: At least one side must be 'eager'.

cards.answer: Same speed, duplex, switchport mode, access VLAN / trunk native and allowed VLANs.
cards.explanation: Mismatched members are suspended (s).
cards.example: show etherchannel summary → Po1(SU) Gi0/1(P) Gi0/2(s)
cards.tip: Clone the config on every member.

cards.front: How is the root bridge elected?
cards.answer: Lowest bridge ID: priority (default 32768 + VLAN ID), then lowest MAC.
cards.explanation: Priority is configured in multiples of 4096.
cards.example: spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary

cards.answer: Lowest root path cost → lowest neighbor bridge ID → lowest neighbor port priority → lowest neighbor port number.
cards.explanation: Every non-root switch has exactly one root port.
cards.example: Two equal-cost uplinks: the one toward the lower bridge ID wins.
cards.tip: Cost, then Bridge ID, then Port.

cards.answer: 10 Mbps 100 • 100 Mbps 19 • 1 Gbps 4 • 10 Gbps 2
cards.explanation: Root path cost = sum of costs of ingress ports along the path.
cards.example: Two 1G hops to root = cost 8.

cards.answer: Discarding, Learning, Forwarding
cards.explanation: Legacy 802.1D: Blocking, Listening, Learning, Forwarding, Disabled.
cards.example: Alternate ports are discarding.

cards.answer: Root, Designated, Alternate, Backup (and Disabled)
cards.explanation: Alternate = backup path to root; Backup = redundant port to the same segment.
cards.example: Blocked uplink on access switch = Alternate.
cards.tip: Alternate → another switch; Backup → same switch/segment.

cards.answer: PortFast skips listening/learning on edge ports; BPDU Guard err-disables the port if a BPDU arrives.
cards.explanation: Use on access ports to end hosts only.
cards.example: spanning-tree portfast / spanning-tree bpduguard enable
cards.tip: Fast for hosts; Guard against switches.

cards.answer: Root Guard: port can't become root port (root-inconsistent). Loop Guard: port stops if BPDUs stop arriving (loop-inconsistent).
cards.explanation: Root Guard on ports toward access switches; Loop Guard on non-designated ports.
cards.example: A rogue switch with priority 0 is blocked by Root Guard.
cards.tip: Root Guard protects WHO is root; Loop Guard protects against missing BPDUs.

cards.answer: SW3's port toward SW2 (alternate/discarding)
cards.explanation: SW1 is root; SW2 has the lower bridge ID so it owns the designated port on the SW2-SW3 segment.
cards.example: Lower bridge ID wins designated-port ties.

cards.answer: Hello 2 s • Forward delay 15 s • Max age 20 s
cards.explanation: Convergence up to 50 s in legacy STP; RSTP converges in seconds.
cards.example: Root sends hellos every 2 s.

cards.answer: 1) Longest prefix match 2) Lowest administrative distance 3) Lowest metric
cards.explanation: AD and metric only matter between routes to the SAME prefix.
cards.example: 10.1.1.0/24 beats 10.1.0.0/16 regardless of AD.

cards.front: Routing table codes C, L, S, S*, O
cards.answer: Connected • Local (/32 interface IP) • Static • Static default (candidate default) • OSPF
cards.explanation: L routes are host routes for the router's own interface addresses.
cards.example: L 10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, Gi0/0

cards.answer: OSPF route, AD 110, metric (cost) 3, next hop 10.0.0.2, exit Gi0/1
cards.explanation: Format [AD/metric].
cards.example: A static would show [1/0].

cards.answer: A backup static with AD set higher than the primary route's AD.
cards.explanation: Installed only when the primary route disappears.

cards.front: IPv6 static route with link-local next hop
cards.answer: Must include the exit interface: ipv6 route ::/0 Gi0/1 FE80::2
cards.explanation: Link-local addresses are only unique per link.

cards.answer: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 <next-hop> • ipv6 route ::/0 <next-hop>
cards.explanation: Shown as S* and 'Gateway of last resort'.

cards.answer: Distance vector shares routes with neighbors (RIP, EIGRP is advanced DV); link state shares topology (LSAs) and runs SPF (OSPF, IS-IS).
cards.explanation: Link-state routers each build a full map of the area.
cards.example: OSPF floods LSAs; RIP sends its table every 30 s.
cards.tip: DV = rumors from neighbors; LS = everyone has the map.

cards.answer: RIP: DV, hop count (max 15), AD 120 • EIGRP: advanced DV, Cisco, composite metric, AD 90 • OSPF: link state, cost, AD 110 • BGP: path vector, AD 20/200
cards.explanation: CCNA v1.1 configures only OSPFv2; others are recognized for comparison.
cards.example: A route learned by EIGRP and OSPF → EIGRP (90) wins.
cards.tip: Only OSPF is configured on the exam.

cards.answer: HSRP: Cisco, active/standby • VRRP: standard, master/backup • GLBP: Cisco, load-balancing AVG/AVFs
cards.explanation: All provide a virtual gateway IP.
cards.example: Multi-vendor site → VRRP.

cards.answer: Down → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full
cards.explanation: DROTHERs stay 2-Way with each other.
cards.example: show ip ospf neighbor: FULL/DR
cards.tip: Don't Invite 2 Extra Exhausted Lazy Friends.

cards.front: What must match for OSPF neighbors?
cards.answer: Area ID, subnet/mask, Hello & Dead timers, authentication, stub flag; unique router IDs; MTU for Full
cards.explanation: Process ID does NOT need to match.
cards.example: Timer mismatch → never neighbors.

cards.answer: 1) router-id command 2) highest loopback IP 3) highest active physical interface IP
cards.explanation: Changed RID requires 'clear ip ospf process'.
cards.example: router-id 1.1.1.1

cards.answer: Highest interface priority (default 1, 0 = never), then highest RID. Non-preemptive.
cards.explanation: Only on broadcast/NBMA networks; none on point-to-point.
cards.example: ip ospf priority 255 on the intended DR.
cards.tip: Highest wins in OSPF (opposite of STP).

cards.answer: Cost = reference bandwidth (100 Mbps default) / interface bandwidth
cards.explanation: FastEthernet and faster all get cost 1 by default; change with auto-cost reference-bandwidth.
cards.example: auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000 → 1G = 10, 10G = 1.

cards.front: OSPF Hello/Dead timers and multicast groups
cards.answer: Hello 10 s, Dead 40 s (broadcast & P2P). 224.0.0.5 all OSPF routers, 224.0.0.6 DR/BDR.
cards.explanation: Dead = 4× Hello by default.
cards.example: DROTHERs send updates to 224.0.0.6.

cards.answer: Stops OSPF Hellos on an interface while still advertising its network.
cards.explanation: Use on user LANs to prevent rogue adjacencies.
cards.example: passive-interface g0/2

cards.answer: network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0 enables OSPF on interfaces in 10.0.12.0/30.
cards.explanation: Uses a wildcard mask, not a subnet mask. Alternative: ip ospf 1 area 0 under the interface.
cards.example: network 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255 area 0 matches all interfaces.

cards.answer: LSAs describe links → stored in the LSDB → SPF computes shortest paths → best routes enter the routing table.
cards.explanation: All routers in an area have identical LSDBs.
cards.example: Type 1 Router LSA, Type 2 Network LSA (from DR).

cards.answer: Advertises a default route into OSPF (requires a default route in the table unless 'always').
cards.explanation: Common on internet edge routers.
cards.example: R1 has ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 ISP; OSPF spreads it.

cards.front: Standard vs extended ACL numbers and matching
cards.answer: Standard 1-99, 1300-1999: source IP only. Extended 100-199, 2000-2699: protocol, source, destination, ports.
cards.explanation: Named ACLs can be either type.
cards.example: access-list 110 permit tcp any host 10.1.1.10 eq 443

cards.answer: Extended near the source; standard near the destination.
cards.explanation: Standard ACLs can't tell destinations apart, so placing them near the source blocks too much.
cards.example: Block PC1 from Server only → extended inbound on PC1's gateway interface.

cards.answer: Top-down, first match wins, implicit deny any at the end.
cards.explanation: An ACL with only deny statements blocks everything.
cards.example: Line 10 permit any above line 20 deny host X → X is permitted.
access-list 5 permit 172.16.0.0 0.15.255.255

cards.explanation: Shortcuts for exact match and match-all.
cards.example: deny ip host 10.1.1.50 any

cards.front: Apply ACL to interface vs VTY
cards.answer: Interface: ip access-group NAME in|out • VTY lines: access-class NAME in
cards.explanation: One ACL per interface, per direction, per protocol.
cards.example: line vty 0 4 / access-class 5 in
cards.tip: Group on interfaces, class on lines.

cards.front: Diagram: where does a packet to 10.2.2.10 on TCP 22 from 10.1.1.5 match?
cards.answer: Line 20 (deny ip any host 10.2.2.10) — line 10 only permits port 443.
cards.explanation: First matching line decides; processing stops.
cards.example: Port 443 would match line 10 and be forwarded.
cards.tip: Check protocol AND port before moving on.

cards.answer: Inbound filters as packets enter the interface (before routing); outbound as they leave.
cards.explanation: Direction is from the router interface's perspective.
cards.example: ip access-group 101 in on the LAN interface.
cards.tip: Stand inside the router and look at the interface.

cards.answer: RADIUS: UDP 1812/1813, standard, encrypts password only, combines authN/authZ. TACACS+: TCP 49, Cisco, encrypts whole payload, separates AAA, per-command authorization.
cards.explanation: TACACS+ preferred for device admin; RADIUS for network access (802.1X/VPN).
cards.example: Switch admin logins via TACACS+; Wi-Fi users via RADIUS.

cards.answer: enable secret is hashed and takes precedence; enable password is clear text (or type 7).
cards.explanation: service password-encryption only applies weak reversible type 7.
cards.example: enable secret Str0ng!

cards.answer: hostname, ip domain-name, crypto key generate rsa (≥768 bits for v2), local user, login local, transport input ssh

techniques.title: Fast subnetting (block-size / magic number)
techniques.method: Skip full binary conversion. Work only in the 'interesting' octet using the block size (256 − mask octet).
steps: Identify the interesting octet from the prefix: /17-/24 → 3rd, /25-/32 → 4th, /9-/16 → 2nd.
Block size = 256 − mask value in that octet.
Network = largest multiple of the block size ≤ the address's octet value.
Broadcast = network + block − 1 in that octet; later octets become 255.
Earlier octets are copied; later octets are 0 for the network.
/19 → 3rd octet, 3 bits → mask 224 → block 32.

compare.traditional: Convert IP and mask to 32 bits, AND them, convert back

compare.fast: Low once block sizes are memorized

safe: Any single-subnet question with a valid prefix
pitfalls: Using the block size in the wrong octet
Forgetting later octets become 0 / 255

techniques.title: Binary-to-decimal shortcuts
techniques.method: Recognize patterns instead of adding all eight bits: leading-ones values, complements, and nibble splitting.
steps: Leading ones = mask values: 1110 0000 = 224.
If mostly ones, subtract: 1111 1011 = 255 − 4 = 251.
Split into nibbles: high nibble × 16 + low nibble (1010 0101 = 10×16 + 5 = 165).
Decimal → binary: subtract place values 128, 64, 32 … from the left.

example.title: Convert 11110110
steps: Mostly ones → 255 minus the zero bits.
Zero bits are at 8 and 1 → 255 − 9 = 246.

safe: Nibble method is exact for any byte
pitfalls: Misplacing a zero bit when using complements

techniques.title: CIDR calculations
techniques.method: Move between prefix, mask, host count and subnet count using powers of two rather than binary.
steps: Host bits h = 32 − prefix; usable = 2^h − 2.
Mask octet = 256 − 2^(bits remaining in that octet).
Subnets created = 2^(new prefix − old prefix).
Hosts needed → find the first 2^h ≥ hosts + 2.

example.title: How many /27 subnets fit in a /22, and how many hosts each?
steps: 27 − 22 = 5 bits → 2^5 = 32 subnets.
32 − 27 = 5 host bits → 2^5 − 2 = 30 hosts.

pitfalls: Forgetting −2 for hosts (except /31, /32)

techniques.title: Network and broadcast at a glance
techniques.method: Network and broadcast are just the bottom and top of the block that contains the address.
steps: Get block size.
Divide the octet by the block size, drop the remainder, multiply back → network.
Add block − 1 → broadcast.
First usable = network + 1; last usable = broadcast − 1.
Network 10.1.1.128, broadcast 10.1.1.191.
Usable .129 – .190

pitfalls: Answering the network address when the question asks for the first USABLE host

pitfalls: Assuming all 172.x or all 192.x addresses are private

techniques.method: Answer in a fixed order: longest prefix → AD → metric. Filter out non-matching routes first.
steps: Write the destination in your head.
Discard routes whose prefix doesn't contain it.
Of the rest, pick the longest prefix.
Only if prefixes tie, compare AD, then metric.
Read next hop and exit interface from that line.

example.title: Destination 10.10.5.9; routes: O 10.10.0.0/16 [110/5], S 10.10.4.0/22 [1/0], D 10.10.5.0/24 [90/30720], S* 0.0.0.0/0
steps: All match.
Longest = /24 (D).
Answer: the EIGRP route — AD never considered.

pitfalls: Choosing by AD before checking prefix length
Forgetting /22 boundaries (4-7)

questions.question: Same prefix learned by OSPF [110/20] and static [1/0]?
Two OSPF routes to the same prefix: [110/10] and [110/20]?

techniques.title: Identifying wildcard masks
techniques.method: Wildcard = 255 − each mask octet. For a single block: last relevant octet = block size − 1.
steps: Convert prefix to mask.
Subtract each octet from 255.
Check: wildcard octets are always 2^n − 1 (0, 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127, 255) for contiguous blocks.
pitfalls: Using the subnet mask in an ACL/OSPF network statement
Forgetting octets after the interesting one become 255

techniques.title: ACL matching
techniques.method: Walk the list top to bottom; stop at the first match; if nothing matches, it's denied.
steps: Note protocol, source, destination, and port of the packet.
Check each line: protocol → source → destination → port. Any mismatch → next line.
First full match decides.
No match → implicit deny.
Confirm the ACL is applied in the right direction on the interface the packet actually crosses.

example.title: Packet: TCP 10.1.1.5 → 10.2.2.10:22. ACL: 10 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443 • 20 deny tcp any host 10.2.2.10 eq 22 • 30 permit ip any any
steps: Line 10: port 443 ≠ 22 → skip.
Line 20: matches → DENY.

pitfalls: Assuming a later, more specific line can override an earlier match
Forgetting the implicit deny

questions.question: ACL: 10 deny ip host 10.1.1.1 any, 20 permit ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any. Traffic from 10.1.1.2?
ACL: 10 permit ip any any, 20 deny ip host 10.9.9.9 any. Traffic from 10.9.9.9?
ACL containing only 'deny tcp any any eq 23'. UDP 53 traffic?

techniques.title: Distinguishing TCP from UDP
techniques.method: Ask: does the application need guaranteed, ordered delivery or a login session? → TCP. Is it real-time, broadcast-based, or a tiny request/response? → UDP.
steps: Look for reliability words (guaranteed, acknowledged, ordered, session, handshake) → TCP.
Look for real-time/low-overhead words (voice, video, streaming, quick query, broadcast) → UDP.
Memorize the exceptions: DNS uses both; TFTP is UDP; TACACS+ is TCP.

example.title: Which needs TCP: VoIP, file download over FTP, DHCP lease, SNMP poll?
steps: FTP needs reliable transfer → TCP.
VoIP, DHCP, SNMP → UDP.

pitfalls: DNS (both), TFTP (UDP), syslog (UDP by default)

questions.question: Which feature belongs only to TCP?
questions.explanation: UDP has ports and a checksum but no windowing.

techniques.title: Recognizing protocol port numbers
steps: Place the number in a family.
Recall the pair rule: lower = server/poll/auth/control; higher = client/trap/accounting/data.
Check transport with the TCP/UDP rule.

example.title: Port 162?
steps: Family 80-179 → SNMP pair 161/162.
Higher number = trap → UDP 162 SNMP traps.

pitfalls: Mixing 1812 (RADIUS) with 1645 legacy
TACACS+ is TCP

techniques.title: Eliminating incorrect answers
techniques.method: Remove options that are technically impossible, off-topic, or absolute before choosing.
steps: Remove options with invented commands or impossible values (e.g., VLAN 5000, mask 255.255.255.200).
Remove options at the wrong OSI layer or wrong protocol family.
Be wary of absolutes ('always', 'never', 'only') unless the fact is absolute.
Compare the last two against the exact wording of the question.
If 'choose two', make sure the pair is consistent.

example.title: Which command enables OSPF on Gi0/1 in area 0? A) ospf enable area 0 B) ip ospf 1 area 0 C) router ospf area 0 D) network g0/1 area 0
steps: A, C, D are not valid IOS syntax → eliminate.
B is the interface-level command.

compare.traditional: Search for the right answer directly

compare.fast: Raises odds from 25% to 50%+ even when unsure

pitfalls: Over-thinking a correct simple answer

questions.question: Which is a valid VLAN ID?
Which is a valid subnet mask?
questions.explanation: 254 is a valid mask octet and the ones are contiguous.

questions.question: Which protocol works at Layer 2?
questions.explanation: STP runs on bridges/switches at Layer 2.

techniques.title: Identifying keywords in questions
techniques.method: Underline (mentally) the words that change the answer: NOT, BEST, FIRST, MOST, two/three, default, IPv6 vs IPv4, inbound/outbound.
steps: Read the last sentence (the actual question) first.
Mark negatives (NOT, EXCEPT) and quantifiers (two, three).
Mark qualifiers: default, best practice, first step, most secure.
Mark context: IPv6, standard vs Cisco-proprietary, Layer 2 vs Layer 3.
Re-read before submitting.

example.title: 'Which TWO statements about RSTP are NOT true?'
steps: Keywords: TWO, NOT, RSTP (not 802.1D).
Select false statements about RSTP specifically.

pitfalls: Missing 'NOT' and answering the opposite
Answering for IPv4 when the question is IPv6

questions.question: 'Which is NOT a valid RSTP port state?'
'Which protocol is an OPEN STANDARD FHRP?'

techniques.title: Managing exam time
techniques.method: Budget time per question, protect time for simulations, and never let one item consume your margin.
steps: Cisco lists the 200-301 exam as 120 minutes; check the question count shown at the start.
Budget = (minutes − reserve) ÷ questions. Keep ~10 minutes as reserve for lab/simulation items.
Set checkpoints (e.g., at 25%, 50%, 75% of questions) and compare with elapsed time.
Cisco exams generally do not allow returning to previous questions — confirm in the exam tutorial and answer before moving on.
If stuck beyond ~2× budget, eliminate, choose the best remaining option, and move on.

example.title: 120 minutes, 100 questions, 10-minute reserve
steps: (120 − 10) ÷ 100 = 1.1 min ≈ 66 s per question.
Checkpoint: question 50 by ~55 minutes elapsed.

pitfalls: Spending 10+ minutes on one drag-and-drop
Not reading the exam tutorial rules

questions.question: 110 usable minutes for 100 questions → seconds per question?
Checkpoint: after 40 of 100 questions with a 66 s budget, elapsed should be about…
You've spent 3 minutes on a 66-second question. Best action?
options: Eliminate, choose best answer, move on
questions.explanation: Protect your time; returning is generally not possible.

techniques.title: Avoiding common trick-question mistakes
techniques.method: Know the classic traps and check for them deliberately.
steps: Usable vs total addresses (−2).
Longest prefix beats AD.
Wildcard vs subnet mask.
OSPF process ID is local; area must match.
STP lowest wins; OSPF DR highest wins.
auto + auto (DTP) and passive + passive (LACP) fail.
Native VLAN is untagged; voice VLAN is tagged.
RADIUS UDP vs TACACS+ TCP.
IPv6 has no broadcast.
DNS uses TCP and UDP.

example.title: 'Hosts in 10.0.0.0/30?'
steps: Total addresses 4, usable 2.
Trap answer: 4.

pitfalls: Changing a correct answer without a concrete reason

questions.question: OSPF neighbors with process IDs 1 and 10, same area. Neighbors?
OSPF DR: priorities 1 and 50. DR?
questions.explanation: Highest wins (if both present at election).

blocks.title: Why binary
blocks.text: Every IPv4 address and mask is 32 bits. Subnetting decisions happen at bit boundaries, so you need to see an octet as 8 switches.

blocks.title: Key fact
blocks.text: 8 bits make an octet; the largest octet value is 255 (all ones).

blocks.title: Binary → decimal
blocks.text: Add the place values of the 1 bits. 10110010 = 128 + 32 + 16 + 2 = 178.

blocks.title: Decimal → binary
blocks.text: Subtract the largest place value that fits, write 1, continue. 99: 64 (35 left) → 32 (3) → 2 (1) → 1 (0) → 01100011.

blocks.title: Shortcut
blocks.text: Mostly ones? Subtract zeros from 255: 11111101 = 255 − 2 = 253.

blocks.title: What a mask does
blocks.text: Contiguous 1 bits mark the network portion; 0 bits mark the host portion. The mask is applied with a bitwise AND to find the network.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.text: Block = 256 − mask octet. Network = largest multiple of block ≤ address octet; later octets = 0.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.text: Broadcast = network + block − 1 in the interesting octet; later octets = 255.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: 10.5.66.3/22 → block 4 in 3rd octet → network 10.5.64.0 → broadcast 10.5.67.255.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.text: First usable = network + 1; last usable = broadcast − 1 (in the last octet).

blocks.title: Special cases
blocks.text: /31 point-to-point links use both addresses; /32 is a single host route.

blocks.title: Formula
blocks.text: Subnets = 2^s, where s = bits borrowed (new prefix − original prefix).

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: 10.0.0.0/8 split into /12s → 2^4 = 16 subnets.

blocks.title: Formula
blocks.text: Usable hosts = 2^h − 2, h = 32 − prefix.

blocks.title: Process
items: Pick the smallest prefix with 2^h − 2 ≥ hosts
Allocate on the next boundary of that block size
Continue from the next free address
